extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and scholars interested in philosophy, ethics, and the relationship between science and morality
extracted.subtask_description: A magazine-style critical review of evolutionary/agnostic accounts of ethics (chiefly Herbert Spencer and D. Van Buren Denslow), assessing their standards, explanatory power, and practical adequacy for moral guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure and pain as tests of right and wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: Spencer's test: pleasure denotes that the action is favorable, pain that it is unfavorable, to the vitality of the organism; pleasure and pain are the sole and universal tests of right and wrong in conduct. His 'supreme end' is 'increased duration' (and intensity) of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: a mother suckling her child is highest instance because both mother and child gain gratification and life-enhancing satisfaction; conversely, acts causing pain or reducing vitality count as wrong. Critique: this standard yields counterintuitive results (e.g., murderer may be 'partly right' from his perspective if it yields him pleasure/prolongs his life), and fails to capture notions of moral beauty, duty, or obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of conscience, duty, and religious sanction from ethical definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Spencer's scheme, authoritative conscience, duty, virtue, obligation, principle, rectitude of motive, and religious sanction do not enter into his definitions or form parts of his system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: actions purely pleasant are judged absolutely right; moral qualities traditionally associated with 'moral beauty' are absent. The reviewer argues this omission strips ethical systems of what we commonly consider their moral character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relativity of pleasure and absence of a universal ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is relative to the organism; there is no such thing as a type or ideal of perfection that fixes a single moral standard across beings or societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: different organisms or social types may have divergent 'right' actions; criticism notes that this undermines the possibility of precise ethical rules and makes moral judgment dependent on organism-specific valuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral precepts as doctrines of the strong
rubrics_metrics.description: Denslow's sociological critique: moral rules are initially impressed by the strong, dominant, and successful upon the weak; many moral precepts (e.g., 'Thou shalt not steal') are class laws devised to protect the interests of property-holders and the ruling forces in society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and illustrations: parable of two sets of swine, property-holders vs non-property-holders; the idea that laws are created and named 'divine' by those who profit. Guidance: treat claims about universality skeptically and analyze whose interests a moral precept serves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceit and truth-telling judged by natural utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Denslow argues nature often makes false impressions first; deceit (e.g., feigning lameness by a partridge) is a natural faculty aiding survival, so truth-telling need not be a universal virtue deducible from nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: military feints, advertising, polite business falsehoods, maternal partridge feigning injury. Use this as a test: does an asserted moral virtue have clear natural utility, or is it a social imposition?

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical systems must yield private-duty guidance ('Is it right?')
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard for adequacy: an ethical system should do more than recommend self-preservation/business-like conduct; it must raise and address the question 'Is it right?' and give guidance for private duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of Spencer: reducing ethics to promotion of one's own interests removes the distinctively moral question and leaves only business-like or biological behavior. An adequate ethical theory should illuminate private moral obligations, not merely prescribe self-promoting actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: The life of the social organism should (or is claimed to) rank above individual lives
rubrics_metrics.description: Spencer's sociological canon: 'the life of the social organism must, as a rule, rank above the lives of its units.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer notes this is asserted dogmatically and insufficiently demonstrated. Use as a criterion by asking whether the theory provides argument/evidence for privileging collective welfare over individual welfare in concrete cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capability to resolve moral dilemmas and medium cases
rubrics_metrics.description: An ethical theory should enable determinate choice in cases where alternatives are both serious; Spencer's pleasure/pain calculus fails in many medium cases because contingencies and probabilistic outcomes can't be reliably calculated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative dilemmas: a merchant deciding whether to borrow to avoid failure (risking lender) and a tenant who must choose between political principle and family welfare (risk of eviction). The reviewer emphasizes the 'hopelessly bewildering calculation' problem as a practical defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality vs class-specific scope of moral maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: A test of a moral precept is whether it is genuinely universal or merely reflects and enforces the interests of a particular class (property-holders, the strong).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Thou shalt not steal' as meaningful and protective for property-holders but not universal for those deprived of property. Use historical and sociological analysis to determine scope and origin of precepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria derived from 'perfection of evolution' (Spencer's positive markers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spencer's list of characteristics associated with 'perfection' in evolution and used as ethically relevant markers: 'adjustment of an action to an end,' 'definiteness,' 'exactness,' 'heterogeneity,' 'complexity,' 'multiformity,' subordination of immediate to remote objects, and of presentative to representative and re-representative sensations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer challenges these as morally neutral or even dangerous: exemplary figures (Napoleon, Ravaillac) may display these attributes yet perform morally heinous acts. Guidance: beware equating technical/teleological 'efficiency' with moral worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of reducing ethics to mere business/self-preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: For an act to have moral quality, it must raise the question 'Is it right?' Mere attention to businesslike self-preservation or function (what is 'clearly essential to self-preservation') does not suffice as morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer uses this as a normative standard: ethical systems that equate morality with fitness-preserving behavior fail to capture distinctive moral considerations; they become indistinguishable from natural biology or commerce.
